FrMS88-de2375-d1e111.summary: Poses the fifth question: whether one formal notion said in quid of God and creature is repugnant to divine perfection. The argument that it is: according to Dionysius, God is eminently above all things.
claims: Divine eminence seems to exclude a common quidditative notion.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e122.summary: Contrary: through eminence we come to knowledge of God by attributing every perfection to him.
claims: The way of eminence attributes every perfection to God.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e129.summary: Raises four logical difficulties, the first being that univocal being would seem to be a genus, since it would be in many and predicated in quid.
claims: Objection: a univocal being said in quid would be a genus.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e138.summary: Second logical difficulty: according to Dionysius, having the notion of a part is repugnant to God, so also is having the notion of something subjectible (a subjective part under being).
claims: Objection: God cannot be a subjective part of being.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e144.summary: Third logical difficulty: some formal notion would then seem prior to deity.
claims: Objection: univocal being would be prior to deity.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e151.summary: Fourth logical difficulty: in essential order the prior is that from which the consequence of subsisting does not convert; with univocal being the consequence from being to divine being does not convert, so deity would not be first. Confirmed: being would then be simpler than God, so something outside the intellect would be simpler than God.
claims: Objection: univocal being would be prior to and simpler than God.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e164.summary: Reply: some say being is contracted by intrinsic modes and so is not a genus. Better, anticipating a later account, being is predicated neither in quid directly nor as an essential part; its predication is closer to that of a genus of a difference than of a genus of a species. Hence being, not being an essential part, is not a genus.
claims: Being is not predicated in quid directly nor as an essential part.
Predication of being resembles predication of a genus of a difference.
Being is not a genus.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e182.summary: Reply to the second difficulty: among transcendentals there are no subjective parts properly speaking.
claims: Transcendentals have no proper subjective parts.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e187.summary: Reply to the third difficulty (labelled 'second' in the text): deity is entirely prior to being, since being is not predicated in quid nor is an essential part.
claims: Deity is prior to the common notion of being.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e194.summary: Reply to the fourth difficulty: the rule fails for consequents not of the quiddity — 'more perfect than a stone' follows from being a man, yet being a man is understood first. Nor is entity in every instant (signum) in which deity is, since in the instant where the divine essence is understood as root of all divine perfections it is not; a naturally prior consequent follows in every instant. Then raises natural difficulties: univocal being seems to destroy creation, since what pre-exists cannot be created, and likewise annihilation, though the whole creature is annihilated.
claims: The non-convertibility rule for priority does not apply to non-quidditative consequents.
Deity as root of all divine perfections is prior to entity in God.
Objection: a pre-existing common notion of being seems incompatible with creation and annihilation.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e224.summary: Reply: whatever is in a creature is created and annihilated as numerically the same, but not everything of the same formal notion must be annihilated — as with a species having a unity in two individuals, one of which can be annihilated while the other remains; a fortiori for transcendentals. Alternatively, quiddity as such is neither produced from nothing nor annihilated but abstracts from these. Then raises a metaphysical difficulty: everything is dependent or independent; if being is dependent it is not in God, if independent not in creatures.
claims: Annihilating a creature does not annihilate what is of the same formal notion elsewhere.
Quiddity as such abstracts from production and annihilation.
Objection: being must be dependent or independent.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e248.summary: Reply: the formal notion of being is neither dependent nor independent, just as substance is neither corporeal nor incorporeal; in God it is independent and in creatures dependent, while in itself it abstracts from both. Then introduces theological difficulties, the first being that the creator is infinitely distant from creatures, so they cannot agree in one notion.
claims: The formal notion of being abstracts from dependence and independence.
Objection: infinite distance excludes a common notion.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e266.summary: Second theological difficulty: whatever is formally 'this' of itself cannot be common to many, and everything in God is of itself formally 'this'.
claims: Objection: whatever is in God is of itself singular and so not common.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e273.summary: Third theological difficulty: no common concept can be abstracted from the simply simple or the primarily diverse, and God and creature are such.
claims: Objection: God and creature are simply simple and primarily diverse, so share no concept.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e280.summary: Fourth theological difficulty: no common concept can be abstracted from contradictory extremes, and God and creature are such (being from itself and not from itself, from another and not from another).
claims: Objection: God and creature are contradictory extremes.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e289.summary: Reply to the first: distance here means only quantity of power; infinite distance shows excess in power but not difference in quidditative notion.
claims: Infinite distance between God and creatures concerns power, not quidditative notion.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e299.summary: Reply to the second: some notions in God are communicable and none of them is of itself 'this' — being is such; others are incommunicable, like infinity, which perhaps is of itself 'this'.
claims: Communicable divine notions such as being are not of themselves individual.
Infinity is perhaps of itself individual in God.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e310.summary: Reply to the third: if being were an essential and quidditative part, the argument would be difficult.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e315.summary: Continues: but, as will be explained later, being is not an essential or quidditative part, so the argument does not tell against Meyronnes.
claims: Being is not an essential or quidditative part.

FrMS88-de2375-d1e322.summary: Completes the replies: God may perhaps be primarily diverse from creatures as regards deity but not as regards the pure perfections in God. To the fourth: abstraction from contradictory extremes is impossible formally but possible fundamentally; God and creature are contradictory fundamentally, not formally, like whiteness and blackness. To the opening argument: God is eminently every creature, containing each more perfectly than it is in itself according to its specific notion.
claims: God may be primarily diverse from creatures in deity but not in pure perfections.
God and creature are contradictory fundamentally, not formally.
God contains every creature eminently, more perfectly than it is in itself.

FrMS88-de2375.summary: The fifth question of the prologue asks whether one formal notion said quidditatively (in quid) of God and creature is repugnant to divine perfection, and answers the difficulties that univocity of being seems to raise, grouped as logical, natural, metaphysical, and theological. Logical: being would be a genus, God would be a subjective part, some notion would be prior to deity, and being would be simpler than God. Meyronnes replies that being is not predicated in quid directly nor as an essential part (its predication resembles that of a genus of a difference), so it is not a genus, transcendentals have no proper subjective parts, and deity is wholly prior. Natural: being, pre-existing, could not be created or annihilated; he answers that what is created or annihilated is the numerically same thing, not everything of the same notion, and quiddity as such abstracts from production. Metaphysical: being must be dependent or independent; he replies that its formal notion is neither, as substance is neither corporeal nor incorporeal, being independent in God and dependent in creatures. Theological: infinite distance, God's being 'of itself this', the simply simple and primarily diverse, and contradictory extremes. He answers that infinite distance is in power, not in quidditative notion; communicable notions in God like being are not of themselves 'this', unlike infinity; God may be primarily diverse in deity but not in pure perfections; and God and creature are contradictory fundamentally, not formally. God contains every creature eminently.
claims: A univocal notion of being said of God and creatures is not repugnant to divine perfection.
Being is not predicated quidditatively in the direct way nor as an essential part, and so is not a genus.
The formal notion of being is neither dependent nor independent; it is independent in God and dependent in creatures.
Infinite distance between God and creatures concerns power, not quidditative notion.
In God, communicable notions such as being are not of themselves individual, whereas infinity perhaps is.
God and creatures are contradictory fundamentally, not formally.
